extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Montaigne / early-modern moral essays; readers interested in ethics, parenting, honour, and practical wisdom
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Michel de Montaigne's essays (moral and personal reflections) with emphasis on normative claims about honour, valour, parenting, age, and domestic conduct. The page contains prescriptive and descriptive principles rather than a formal rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity preserves honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Honour is a privilege which derives its principal essence from rarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the value of honour depends on few people enjoying it, liberal and widespread distribution brings it down to nothing. Honour as a recompense should be rare to retain esteem; making it common cheapens its worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep honour separate from material gain
rubrics_metrics.description: If with the reward, which ought to be simply a recompense of honour, they should mix other commodities and add riches, this mixture... would debase and abate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orders or distinctions that carry money or material advantage lose dignity because money is used for many common transactions (wages, services, even to reward vice). Example: the Order of St. Michael retained esteem because it had no material commodity attached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional honours require strict rules to avoid dilution
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules for dispensing this new order had need to be extremely clipt and bound under great restrictions, to give it authority; and this tumultuous season is incapable of such a curb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New orders or honours introduced in troubled times risk rapid debasement unless governed by tight, restrictive rules and the memory of prior contempt buried. Anti-pattern: creating broad honours without strict selection will ruin their value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue loses esteem when it becomes common custom
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no recompense becomes virtue, how great soever, that is once passed into a custom... I do not think that any citizen of Sparta glorified himself much upon his valour, it being the universal virtue of the whole nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a virtue or deed becomes universal or customary, it ceases to be especially commended. Historical examples: Spartan citizens, communal virtues in certain nations. Implication: scarcity underpins esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recompense military leadership, not mere soldiery
rubrics_metrics.description: Recompense... never was the reward of a valiant soldier but of a great captain; the science of obeying was not reputed worthy of so honourable a guerdon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honours for military merit should recognise universal military expertness and leadership (generalship), not merely bravery in obedience. Anti-pattern: awarding high orders for commonplace brave acts diminishes their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: True and regular parental affection should grow with knowledge and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A true and regular affection ought to spring and increase with the knowledge they give us of themselves, and then, if they are worthy of it, the natural propension walking hand in hand with reason, to cherish them with a truly paternal love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive early caressing of newborns who 'have as yet neither motion of soul nor shape of body distinguishable.' Affection should be guided by judgment and the child's demonstrated qualities rather than blind instinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include children in sharing goods and domestic affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: It is cruelty and injustice not to receive them into the share and society of our goods, and not to make them partakers in the intelligence of our domestic affairs when they are capable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fathers should lessen and contract their own expenses to make room for their children's advancement. Hoarding wealth so children lack means can drive them to despair or dishonourable actions (e.g., theft). Share resources and inform capable children of domestic matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect should be earned by virtue and wisdom, not by dependence on assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: A father is very miserable who has no other hold on his children’s affection than the need they have of his assistance; he must render himself worthy to be respected by his virtue and wisdom, and beloved by his kindness and the sweetness of his manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority based solely on material necessity breeds a poor form of 'affection'. Parents should cultivate moral authority and kindness rather than rely on power derived from providing support alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate by reason and gentleness; avoid corporal punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: I condemn all violence in the education of a tender soul that is designed for honour and liberty... what is not to be done by reason, prudence, and address, is never to be affected by force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author practised minimal corporal punishment; experience shows whipping tends to make boys more cowardly or more obstinate. Anti-pattern: harshness and constraint are servile and counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not marry so young that parental age conflicts with children
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us not marry so young that our age shall in a manner be confounded with theirs... I married at three-and-thirty years of age, and concur in the opinion of thirty-five, which is said to be that of Aristotle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing appropriate age for marriage avoids difficulties where parents become too close in age to their offspring; younger fathers may impede the proper generational distinction and duties (e.g., military service). Historical views referenced (Plato, Aristotle, Thales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elders should resign possessions/power when feeble
rubrics_metrics.description: The Emperor Charles V. ... resigned his possessions, grandeur, and power to his son, when he found himself failing in vigour... 'Dismiss the old horse in good time, lest, failing in the lists, the spectators laugh.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When age impairs competence, voluntarily giving up central house/power and enabling successors preserves dignity and the family's well-being. Anti-pattern: clinging to possessions leads to imbecility, suspicion, and domestic ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fathers should cultivate familiarity and be accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is folly and injustice to deprive children, when grown up, of familiarity with their father, and to carry a scornful and austere countenance toward them... Though I could make myself feared, I had yet much rather make myself beloved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For lasting influence in old age, being beloved is preferable to maintaining authority by fear; forbidding children to call 'father' or enforcing excessive distance produces ridicule and alienation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep some supervision but allow children practical management and revocation rights
rubrics_metrics.description: I would resign to them the enjoyment of my house and goods, but with a power of revocation if they should give me cause to alter my mind... to put his children into the way of governing his affairs, and to have power during his own life to control their behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical compromise: hand over use and governance to children while retaining ultimate oversight to instruct and correct, and live near enough to observe and cultivate friendship without being a nuisance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of household corruption and prefer true friends over civil ties
rubrics_metrics.description: So many servants, so many enemies... wife, son, and servant, are so many enemies to us?... I protect myself from such treasons in my own bosom, not by an unquiet and tumultuous curiosity, but rather by diversion and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old people are prone to deception by household members; cultivate trustworthy friendships and self-awareness rather than suspicious micromanagement. Use observation of others' misfortunes as caution for oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: True philosophical virtue is steady, learnable, and cultivable by education
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another virtue... much greater than this and more full, which is a force and assurance of the soul, equally despising all sorts of adverse accidents, equable, uniform, and constant... Use, education, example, and custom can do all in all to the establishment of that whereof I am speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish military valour (a 'ray') from a deeper, philosophical steadiness of soul; this higher virtue can be taught and made common by education and custom, which explains how military reputation can be revived by collective enterprise.
